blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A pole type has shape 3 and scale 40 years. One pole of that type is 50 years old and still standing. An analyst reports its chance of failing in the coming year as F(51) - F(50) = 1.6%. What should the report say instead?

options.text: Nothing else, since F(51) - F(50) is the chance this standing pole fails within the year
options.says: F(51) - F(50) is the share of a new fleet that fails in that year; most of that fleet failed earlier, so it understates the risk of a pole that is standing.

options.text: F(50) = 86%, since the curve at age 50 is the chance this standing pole fails within the year
options.says: F(50) is the chance of having failed at some point before age 50, counted from new, not of failing during the coming year.

options.text: The same difference divided by R(50) = 14%, since the pole is known to be standing at age 50
options.says: Right: given that it stands at 50, PoF = (F(51) - F(50)) / R(50), about 11%.

options.text: The hazard h(50), since a hazard is the chance this standing pole fails within the year
options.says: A hazard is a rate per year among units still working; it can exceed 1, so it is not a probability.

origin.section: Next Year's PoF Is Conditional on the Asset Working Today

questions.stem: The reliability team reports that one cable type has a Weibull shape of 0.8. A planner proposes replacing the oldest cables of that type first, to cut failures. What does the shape say about the proposal?

options.text: Old cables of this type fail at a lower rate than young ones, so new cables raise the rate
options.says: Right: with a shape below 1 the hazard falls with age (infant mortality), so a new cable is riskier than an old survivor.

options.text: Old cables of this type fail at a higher rate than young ones, so new cables cut the rate
options.says: That is a shape above 1, the wear-out pattern; below 1 the hazard falls with age.

options.text: Cables of this type fail at the same rate at every age, so new cables leave it alone
options.says: A constant hazard is the shape-1 case only; at 0.8 the rate falls with age.

options.text: Cables of this type fail at a rate that peaks at the scale, so new cables help after it
options.says: A Weibull hazard is a power of age with no peak; at a shape of 0.8 it falls at every age.

origin.section: The Hazard Is the Failure Rate Among the Assets Still Working

questions.stem: Two breaker types both have a scale of 50 years. Type K has shape 1.5 and type L has shape 5. By what age have 63% of each type failed?

options.text: By the scale for L and well after it for K, since a small shape spreads the lives out
options.says: F(eta) = 1 - 1/e for every shape, so both types reach 63% at 50 years.

options.text: By the scale for K and well after it for L, since a large shape pushes the failures late
options.says: F(eta) = 1 - 1/e for every shape, so both types reach 63% at 50 years.

options.text: By each type's mean life, which differs by shape, since 63% fail before the mean life
options.says: The scale is not the mean; the mean is eta times Gamma(1 + 1/beta) and the 63% age is eta.

options.text: By the scale for both types, since the share failed at the scale does not depend on shape
options.says: Right: at t = eta the exponent is -1 for every shape, so F(eta) is about 0.632 for both.

origin.section: Beta Is the Shape, and Eta Is the Age by Which 63% Have Failed
